title: Phrasal verbs for writing
intro: Not every phrasal verb is too informal for an essay. The forty-five below are used freely in reports, articles and academic writing, so you can use them in an IELTS answer without losing marks. Each one comes with its meaning, an example and, where a good one exists, a single more formal word you can swap in. A natural phrasal verb you control is always better than a formal word you are guessing at.

tables.caption: Phrasal verbs for writing: A–L
rows: be the cause of, or make up a share of
Tourism **accounts for** almost a third of the city's income.
The extra fees **add up to** nearly two million đồng a year.
Most complaints **arise from** poor communication with parents.
The report **is based on** a survey of five hundred students.
separate something into parts so it can be studied
The article **breaks** the process **down** into four stages.
The new rule **brought about** a sharp fall in accidents.
develop something further from an earlier base
This study **builds on** earlier research carried out in Đà Nẵng.
do or perform research, a plan or an order
The team **carried out** interviews in three districts.
provide what a particular group needs
The library **caters for** both students and teachers.
have something as the main focus
The debate **centred on** the cost of the new bridge.
We **came across** two studies that reached the same conclusion.
The course **consists of** eight units and a final project.
help to cause or to improve something
Motorbike traffic **contributes to** poor air quality in the centre.
The canteen has **cut down on** single-use plastic since March.
handle a problem, or be about a subject
Chapter two **deals with** renewable energy in rural areas.
be decided by, or need in order to succeed
The result **depends on** the size of the sample.
The essay **draws on** data from two government reports.
prepare a plan, a list or a contract
The committee **drew up** a timetable at the end of March.
Fewer students **engage in** sport at the weekend than ten years ago.
The answers **fall into** three clear categories.
give your attention to one thing
This section **focuses on** schools in the Mekong Delta.
Rapid building on the riverbank has **given rise to** flooding.
examine something carefully from start to finish
**Go through** your draft once looking only at verb forms.
give a piece of work to a teacher or an office
Please **hand in** the application form before Friday.
stay level with something that is moving or changing
Wages have not **kept up with** the price of housing.
Longer journeys to school **lead to** lower attendance.
examine a problem in order to find out more
The council is **looking into** the noise around the market.

tables.caption: Phrasal verbs for writing: M–W
rows: Girls **make up** fifty-five per cent of the class.
choose one thing rather than another
Most families **opt for** the cheaper package.
draw the reader's attention to a fact
The writer **points out** that the figures are five years old.
offer an idea for other people to consider
She **put forward** three explanations for the drop in sales.
mention something, or send the reader to it
The chart **referred to** in the introduction is on page four.
need something or someone in order to succeed
Small shops **rely on** customers from the same street.
The delay **resulted from** a shortage of trained staff.
The new timetable **resulted in** much shorter queues.
decide that something is not possible
We cannot **rule out** a second cause for the flooding.
explain something in an organised way
The introduction **sets out** the aims of the project.
start an organisation or a system
The reading club **was set up** in 2018 by two teachers.
The problem **stems from** planning decisions made in the 1990s.
**To sum up**, the scheme is worth extending for another year.
consider something when you make a decision
The plan **takes** the rainy season **into account**.
Teachers have **taken on** two extra classes each this term.
gain control of a company or a job
A larger firm **took over** the factory in 2020.
prove to be true, or to be the case
The first set of results **turned out** to be wrong.
calculate something, or find a solution
**Work out** the average before you compare the two groups.

notes: Some of these split around their object and some never do. You can write *carry the survey out* or *carry out the survey*, and *take the season into account*; but *consist of*, *depend on*, *refer to*, *rely on* and *result in* always keep their preposition next to the verb.
When a phrasal verb is separable and the object is a pronoun, the pronoun goes in the middle: *the committee drew **it** up*, never *drew up it*.

A one-word alternative is not automatically better. *Carry out a survey* is completely normal in academic writing, while a formal word used slightly wrongly is far more noticeable than a well-chosen phrasal verb.

Keep these for speaking and informal emails: *put up with*, *sort out*, *figure out*, *check out*, *get rid of*, *come up with*, *find out*. In an essay use *tolerate*, *resolve*, *determine*, *examine*, *remove*, *propose* and *discover*.
After any of these prepositions, a verb takes -ing: *the plan depends on **raising** more money*, *she succeeded in **finishing** on time*.
